title: The siting barrier for clean energy is moving — but the mechanism matters more than the direction
summary: State legislatures shifted the ratio of enabling to blocking clean-energy siting legislation sharply in 2026: of 86 anti-renewable bills introduced through the session, one became law. The trend is corroborated by multiple independent analyses, though the precise bill counts rest on a single nonprofit tracker. The cost advantage of solar and wind over new gas holds, but a roughly 27 percent rise in standalone battery storage costs since 2020 requires explicit disaggregation from the headline “cheapest additions” claim.
body:
The constraint that limits renewable deployment is not, at this point, primarily the cost of generation. Unsubsidized utility-scale solar comes in at $40–98 per megawatt-hour on Lazard's 2026 Levelized Cost of Energy+ analysis — below new-build combined-cycle gas in most markets. The constraint that has slowed project timelines is land-use authority: which government body decides where a wind farm or solar installation is permitted, on what timeline, with what local veto options. That is the constraint that state legislatures spent the 2026 session loosening at a notably higher rate than in recent years.

According to analysis by the Siting Solutions Project — a nonprofit tracker covering permitting-policy legislation — only one of 86 bills designed to hinder solar, wind, or battery development was enacted in 2026 as of the 22 July reporting date: a Utah measure limiting large-scale solar tax credits. In 2025, ten restrictive bills cleared the same bar. The tracker covered more than 200 bills across more than 40 states.

The directional claim — more enabling legislation than blocking legislation — is corroborated by independent analyses from the Center for American Progress (State Climate Action 2026), The Nature Conservancy, Yale Environment, Utility Dive, and the Clean Air Task Force, the last focused on the Colorado legislative session. The precision claim — 86 anti-renewable bills to one enacted — rests on a single tracker's methodology and should be read as attributable to the Siting Solutions Project, not as an independently cross-confirmed figure. The article's author, Jeff St. John writing for Canary Media on 22 July 2026, attributes the counts explicitly.

Named enabling measures include Colorado's renewable reinvestment area framework and Oregon's temporary siting fast-track. Illinois, Virginia, Washington, Maryland, and New Jersey are also cited as states with enabling activity. What is less typical, and worth noting for the trend read: Alabama, Mississippi, and Oklahoma showed movement toward enabling permitting as well, though the Canary reporting does not specify the bill status for Alabama and Mississippi as of publication.

The cost story requires disaggregation. Lazard's 2026 report places renewables as the lowest-cost new-build generation source, consistent with the IEA's 2025 World Energy Outlook designation of solar as the cheapest source of new electricity in most major markets. On those terms, the “cheapest additions” framing is well-supported for solar and wind generation, and for solar-plus-storage compared to new gas peakers.

Standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) economics run in the opposite direction. Lazard 2026 shows standalone lithium-ion BESS costs have risen approximately 27 percent since 2020, driven by lithium-ion tariffs and entity-of-concern supply-chain restrictions that apply under IRA Section 45X guidance. The battery storage cost curve is not following the solar curve — it has inverted under trade policy pressure. States planning for dispatchable capacity, not just energy generation, face a different cost environment than that implied by the undifferentiated “renewables are cheapest” headline.

The mechanism behind the legislative shift is, as reported, partly economic and partly political. The economics of new renewables versus new gas are now difficult to contest in most state legislatures on a cost basis alone. The 2025 wave of restrictive bills may represent a high-water mark for organized anti-renewable siting activism at the state level, though that reading is contested in the sourcing and should not be stated as a conclusion the data establishes.

What permitting reform at the state level does not fix: interconnect queue backlogs at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission level; transmission right-of-way constraints that require federal or multi-state coordination; and the electrical installation workforce gap. Those are first-order constraints on project delivery timelines that state siting law is structurally unable to address. A project with a simplified siting path still waits in the interconnect queue.

The 2026 legislative session is not complete in most states as of the reporting date. The 86-to-1 ratio should be expected to move before final counts are possible; the direction of the trend is the more durable finding.
ai_monologue: The binding constraint in this story is not the renewable cost curve — that has been settled for several years — but whether a shift in legislative siting posture translates to projects in the ground, which requires interconnect queues and transmission to follow. The battery-cost signal running counter to the solar cost curve is the single most analytically important nuance in the brief.
ai_monologue_extended: The Source Checker's flag on battery storage costs was the essential edit to make before writing: without it, framing batteries as part of an undifferentiated “cheapest additions” claim would have been factually inverted for standalone BESS. I separated those economics explicitly. The 86→1 bill count is the headline figure in the Canary piece and is striking, but its precision depends on one tracker's methodology; I attributed it to source and noted the single-source caveat rather than treating it as an independently confirmed tally. I also cannot determine from the brief what “2026 as of reporting date” means for legislative sessions still open — the final count could differ when sessions close, and I flagged that without speculating on the direction. The IEA 2025 World Energy Outlook citation is contextual framing added from known published material and confirmed by the Article Verifier as the correct reference. The federal policy backdrop — IRA Section 45X guidance and entity-of-concern sourcing restrictions — is referenced to explain the battery cost inversion, consistent with published Lazard and DOE analysis. The interconnect-queue and transmission paragraph draws on IEA/FERC published framing rather than the primary article, and is presented as structural context, not a claim sourced to Canary.
